1. Infantry as the Baseline

In most regions for most of this period, infantry (armed with spears, swords, or pikes) typically accounts for the bulk of battlefield deaths—often 40–70%.

2. Ranged Weapons

• In China, the crossbow was unusually important from the Warring States onward.

• In the Middle East, horse archers and foot archers could become quite significant (30–40% of kills) during eras dominated by nomadic or semi-nomadic powers.

• In Europe, archery was less dominant in the Classical/early medieval period but became far more lethal with the longbow and crossbow in the High/Late Middle Ages (could reach 30–40% of battlefield kills in major set-piece battles).

3. Cavalry

• Grows in importance significantly after about 200 CE as empires adapt to steppe threats or develop their own heavy cavalry (e.g., Sasanian cataphracts, Byzantine cavalry, medieval knights).

• In certain contexts (e.g., Mongol conquests, high medieval knights), cavalry could be the deciding factor, though the raw percentage of kills might vary from ~20% up to 50%+ (especially in steppe-dominated engagements).

4. Specialty Arms (Elephants, Chariots)

• Chariots fade into niche or ceremonial roles after 500 BCE in most places except a few holdouts (some Celtic, Indian contexts).

• Elephants see heavy use in India (and occasionally in the Hellenistic and Carthaginian armies) but rarely constitute more than 10–15% of total battlefield kills, despite their psychological impact.

5. Siege vs. Field Battles

• Many casualties in pre-modern warfare actually occurred in sieges (starvation, disease, close-quarters assault). Within a siege, ranged weapons (arrows, stones, etc.) could dominate, while final assaults involved brutal melee.

• The numbers above lean toward open-field battles. If sieges are included, the share of ranged kills might be higher.
